lessons.title: Action Spaces: Discrete Buy/Sell/Hold vs Continuous Position Sizing

body.text: The environment built in the previous lesson used the simplest possible action space, three choices, one lot each. This lesson shows what actually changes in the code, and in the agent's behavior, when that action space is redesigned for finer sizing, continuous exposure, or a completely different way of thinking about what an 'action' even represents.

children.text: Recap: Why Action Space Choice Isn't Free

Chapter 1 compared discrete and continuous action spaces in principle, and Chapter 2 showed that the choice determines which algorithm families are even available: value-based methods like Q-learning fit discrete actions naturally, while policy-based and actor-critic methods are what handle continuous actions well. This lesson makes that choice concrete inside the environment itself, and introduces a third option neither earlier lesson covered: actions defined as a change relative to the current position, rather than an absolute target.
Finer-Grained Discrete Actions: More Than Three Choices

The previous lesson's three-action space, sell, hold, buy, only ever sizes into 1 lot in either direction. A common middle ground keeps the discreteness that value-based algorithms need, while giving the agent more than one size to choose from.

body.caption: Five discrete actions instead of three, each mapping to a fixed position size. The rest of step(), computing trade_size, transaction cost, and the drawdown-penalized reward, needs no changes at all; only how an action maps to a target position changed.

children.text: A Continuous Action Space: Position Size as a Fraction of Maximum Exposure

A continuous action space replaces the fixed list of position levels with a single number the agent outputs directly, scaled to a maximum allowed exposure. This is what a policy-based or actor-critic algorithm from Chapter 2 expects to act on.

body.caption: The agent now outputs a single value between -1 and 1, clipped for safety even though the algorithm should already respect the action space bounds, and scaled to a maximum exposure. Note that target_position is no longer restricted to whole lots. For an instrument that genuinely requires integer lots, an extra rounding step belongs here, with the caveat that rounding can make two nearby continuous actions collapse to an identical trade, quietly reducing the precision the continuous action space was meant to provide.

children.text: Action Smoothing: Why Real Environments Often Penalize Rapid Direction Changes

Any of these action spaces can produce an ugly failure mode early in training: an agent that has not yet learned anything useful flips between buy and sell almost every step, since exploration under an untrained policy is close to random. The transaction cost term in the reward already discourages this, but a poorly tuned cost relative to typical P&L swings, the same tuning risk the previous lesson's reward-design work flagged, can leave the agent flipping anyway during the noisiest early phase of training. Several established techniques reduce this beyond what the transaction cost term alone provides.

cells: The action changes position incrementally rather than jumping to an absolute target
Naturally discourages rapid full reversals, but needs several consecutive actions to reach a large position
Position changes are only allowed every N steps, ignored or penalized otherwise
Simple and effective, but can make the agent miss a genuinely fast-moving opportunity
Larger transaction cost in the reward
Raise the cost coefficient so frequent flipping is priced more heavily
Already built into the environment; effective, but too high a cost can suppress legitimate trading, the same tuning risk the drawdown penalty carries
Fewer, larger position levels instead of many fine-grained ones
Reduces how often the agent flips between adjacent levels, at the cost of sizing precision

children.text: Delta Actions: Changing Position Instead of Setting It

Every action space so far has specified an absolute target position: buy means go to +1 lot, regardless of where the agent currently stands. A delta action space instead specifies a change relative to the current position, closer to how real order placement actually works, one order at a time, building toward a size rather than jumping to it.

body.code:
DELTA_LEVELS = [-1, 0, 1]  # decrease, hold, increase, in lots

class NiftyFuturesEnv(gym.Env):
    def __init__(self, price_data, lookback=10, lot_size=50, max_lots=3, **kwargs):
        super().__init__()
        # ... same setup as the previous lesson ...
        self.max_lots = max_lots
        self.action_space = spaces.Discrete(len(DELTA_LEVELS))

    def step(self, action):
        delta = DELTA_LEVELS[action]
        target_position = int(np.clip(self.position + delta, -self.max_lots, self.max_lots))
        # ... the rest of step() is unchanged from the previous lesson ...
body.caption: Reaching the maximum position of 3 lots now takes three consecutive 'increase' actions rather than one action, which structurally limits how fast the agent can reverse direction, since undoing a large position takes just as many 'decrease' actions to unwind. The clip() call keeps the position within max_lots regardless of how many increase actions are taken in a row.

body.text: Delta actions and coarser action counts both reduce churn by construction, before training even starts, rather than relying entirely on the reward function to discourage it after the fact. Combining a structural constraint with a well-tuned transaction cost is usually more robust than leaning on either one alone.

body.title: Diagnosing Excessive Trading Frequency
body.scenario: An agent trained on the absolute three-action environment from the previous lesson (sell, hold, buy, one lot each) ends up flipping position on roughly 40% of all steps during evaluation, far more than any reasonable Nifty 50 futures strategy would trade intraday, and its net reward is barely positive after transaction costs.
body.prompt: Suggest two different fixes, from two different categories of solution covered in this lesson, and explain what each one actually changes about the agent's behavior.
body.modelAnswer: One fix is structural: switch from an absolute action space to a delta action space, so that flipping from a full long position to a full short position requires several consecutive decrease actions rather than a single action, mechanically limiting how quickly the agent can reverse regardless of what it has learned. A second, independent fix works through the reward rather than the action space: increase the transaction cost coefficient in the reward function, making each flip more expensive in training so the agent has a stronger incentive to learn to hold positions rather than churn them. These are genuinely different levers, one constrains what actions are structurally possible, the other changes what the agent is incentivized to prefer, and they can be applied together rather than as alternatives, since a delta action space still benefits from a properly tuned transaction cost on top of it.

body.title: Matching Action Space to Algorithm
body.question: Based on Chapter 2's distinction between value-based and policy-based methods, which action space design from this lesson would be a poor fit for a plain Q-learning agent, without further modification?
options: The continuous action space using spaces.Box
All of the action spaces in this lesson work equally well with Q-learning
body.explanation: Q-learning, a value-based method, works by estimating Q(s,a) for a finite, enumerable set of actions and choosing the one with the highest value. A continuous action space has infinitely many possible actions, so there is no finite table or simple max operation to fall back on without a further modification, such as discretizing the continuous range or switching to a policy-based or actor-critic method built for continuous control. Both discrete action spaces in this lesson, the five-level and the delta version, plug directly into plain Q-learning with no changes needed.

points: The action space choice made in the previous lesson's environment, three absolute discrete actions, is one option among several, and the rest of step() barely needs to change to support a different one
A finer discrete action space (more position levels) keeps compatibility with value-based algorithms like Q-learning while giving the agent more sizing granularity
A continuous action space, via spaces.Box, is what policy-based and actor-critic algorithms expect, and requires deciding separately whether the resulting position needs to be rounded to whole lots

Excessive action churn, flipping position rapidly during early or poorly tuned training, can be reduced structurally (delta actions, cooldowns, coarser levels) as well as through the reward function's transaction cost term, and combining both is usually more robust than relying on either alone

Delta actions define an action as a change relative to the current position rather than an absolute target, which structurally limits how fast the agent can reverse direction regardless of what its policy has learned

With state, reward, and action space all built and code-tested in this chapter, the environment is ready for the training, validation, and risk-management work that extends this course as further chapters are added
